item.title: Georgia woman celebrates 112th birthday, reveals her secret to a long life
item.description: Mabel Dunbar of Fayetteville, Georgia, turned 112 and says religious faith and close family ties are the secrets behind her remarkable longevity.
item.content:encoded:
A Georgia woman who just celebrated her 112th birthday credits her longevity to staying close to her family and embracing her strong religious faith.

Mabel Dunbar, of Fayetteville, Georgia, was born in Jamaica in 1914. She is the mother of one, grandmother of four and a great-grandmother, and was honored by loved ones on her birthday Sept. 5 with a custom berry cake, flowers and a crown, FOX 5 Atlanta reported.

"God is love and I love my families," Dunbar said at her party. "I love all my families and strangers."

HOW A 93-YEAR-OLD SOCCER REFEREE CREDITS WARTIME RATIONS AND DISCIPLINE FOR HIS LONGEVITY

Those who know her describe Dunbar as "deeply religious, pleasant and talkative," according to FOX 5.

She spent her life serving others and remaining active, the station reported. Until recently, Dunbar still enjoyed cooking and made breakfast for herself every morning. She also enjoyed sharing stories with visitors.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

After moving to Florida to live with her daughter in 1994, Dunbar relocated to Fayetteville in August 2025 to live with her granddaughter and grandson-in-law.

Family remains an important part of Dunbar’s daily life, according to FOX 5.

"Treat them the best you can, because they are important," Dunbar said of younger generations, specifically her grandchildren. "You need them when you can't help yourself like me. These good people are on me all the time, and I'm happy to see them when they come."

Leading oncologist and University of Pennsylvania bioethicist Dr. Ezekiel Emanuel has identified several principles for living longer and reducing disease risk.

They include prioritizing an active social life, staying mentally active with new hobbies and opportunities to learn, limiting processed and sugary foods and drinks without being overly restrictive, engaging in moderate exercise and getting proper sleep, Fox News Digital previously reported.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Emanuel also recommends avoiding obviously dangerous activities and behaviors.

Religious involvement has also been associated with greater longevity, research has suggested.

In a 2016 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine, researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health examined religious service attendance and health outcomes among 74,534 women over 16 years.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

They found that women who attended religious services more than once a week had a 33% lower risk of dying during the follow-up period compared with women who never attended religious services.

Weekly attendance was associated with a 26% lower risk, while attendance less than once a week was associated with a 13% lower risk. Regular attendees also tended to smoke less, experience fewer depressive symptoms and have stronger social support, the researchers reported in 2016.

The world’s oldest documented living person is Ethel Caterham, of England, who turned 117 in August.

Caterham previously told The Associated Press that she credited her long life to "never arguing with anyone," adding, "I listen, and I do what I like."

item.title: Virginia mom placed on child abuse registry for 7 years after letting 5-year-old walk alone
item.description: Karyann Parkinson told "Fox & Friends Weekend" Saturday she's appealing her conviction for contributing to the delinquency of a minor in Virginia.
item.content:encoded:
A Virginia mom is appealing a criminal charge and her placement on the state’s child abuse and neglect registry after her 5-year-old son was stopped by security while walking alone through their gated community.

Karyann Parkinson said her son, Sam, had been walking along a familiar neighborhood path past a pond to collect goose feathers when a security guard encountered him and brought him home.

Police and Child Protective Services became involved, and Parkinson, who was eight months pregnant at the time, had her six-month jail sentence suspended, but the charge remains.

She was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, a first-degree misdemeanor, and was also placed on Virginia's Child Abuse and Neglect Central Registry for seven years.

PARENTS SPEAK OUT AFTER SON WITH AUTISM, 6, WAS SUSPENDED FOR BITING SANDWICH INTO SHAPE OF GUN

Parkinson said she understands the shock people feel hearing about a child alone near a body of water, but sought to clarify what happened that day.

"I didn't send him to play at the pond," she told "Fox & Friends Weekend." "I sent him down the path that happens to go past the pond to collect goose feathers... I know that a lot of people have seen the headlines and seen '5-year-old alone at a pond.' And I think if I saw that in isolation, I'd probably be alarmed, too."

SAN FRANCISCO DAD QUESTIONED BY PARK RANGERS FOR TEACHING HIS OWN KIDS TENNIS AT PUBLIC COURT

"But what this was, was a 5-year-old on a pathway that he's very familiar with in his neighborhood that he loves, the only place that he can remember ever living. And it just got turned into this whole situation where a lot of people were suddenly intervening and feeling like this was a really drastic parenting choice," she said.

The most difficult part for Parkinson is being on the Child Protective Services registry for so long, she told Fox News. That means she won't be able to volunteer in Sam's classroom until he enters sixth grade.

FAMILY STOPPED ALLEGED CHILD KIDNAPPER AS POLICE SAY STAFFING SHORTAGE DELAYED RESPONSE UP TO 40 MINUTES

"We need to stop parenting from a place of fear and a place, you know, of obsessing over the unknown or some boogeyman who's going to jump out from behind a bush," Parkinson said.

She said her son was "pretty shaken up" after the incident but has since recovered.

"We had to do a lot of reassuring him and telling him, 'You didn't do anything wrong,'" Parkinson said. "He would ask me, 'Mom, am I allowed to ride my bike to swim practice? Am I allowed to ride my back to the tennis courts?'"

"Now it's just a blip on his radar. It's not really a part of his life anymore," she added.

item.title: Hikers stranded on Mount Shasta after relying on AI to plan trip, sheriff says
item.description: Three Roseville hikers used Google's Gemini AI to plan a Mount Shasta climb but ended up stranded overnight in a steep canyon, authorities said.
item.content:encoded:
A trio of novice hikers who turned to AI to help plan their climb up California’s Mount Shasta ended up stranded overnight in a steep canyon after their trek went dangerously off course, authorities said.

The three young men from Roseville told a Siskiyou County sheriff’s deputy after their rescue that they had relied heavily on Google Gemini for information about the route and what to pack for the trip.

That proved to be a "critical misstep," the sheriff’s office said, because Gemini advised them to bring far less food and water than they needed when their planned eight-hour ascent stretched into a multi-day ordeal.

CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER

The hikers made camp at about 8,400 feet on Saturday, Aug. 29, then set out with daypacks for the summit at 3 a.m. Sunday.

They did not reach the top until 7 p.m. — seven hours after the recommended noon turnaround time — leaving them to descend in the dark.

About an hour later, the hikers called the sheriff’s office for directions but eventually wandered off the Clear Creek Route and into Mud Creek Canyon.

One of the men later fell and injured his knee, stranding the group in the steep canyon overnight.

U.S. Forest Service climbing rangers reached the hikers the next morning and treated the injured man. Siskiyou County Search and Rescue volunteers also were sent to help, and everyone made it back to the trailhead safely.

MISSOURI DEPUTY AG, MISSING 6 DAYS AFTER SEEKING TO SUMMIT WYOMING'S TALLEST PEAK, IS FOUND ALIVE

"It is always advisable to call the local USFS Mount Shasta Ranger Station ahead of your trip to ensure you have the most accurate information, and to never rely solely on AI for your trip planning," the sheriff’s office said.

Climbers who have not reached the summit by noon should turn back, the sheriff’s office said, giving themselves — and rescuers, if needed — enough daylight to get off the mountain.

Hikers should also carry more than one way to navigate and regularly check that they are still on the correct route rather than depending on a cellphone or GPS device.

The Clear Creek Route does not require technical mountaineering, but hikers still need to be fit and prepared for injuries, bad weather or an unexpected night on the mountain, the sheriff’s office said.

Serious accidents and deaths have occurred when people became lost and wandered into more dangerous areas such as the Mud Creek drainage.

item.title: Democrat challenging Mike Lawler won't commit on campaigning with AOC, Mamdani or rejecting DSA
item.description: Cait Conley said she won't campaign with Zohran Mamdani or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez but stopped short of rejecting the DSA on national television.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic U.S. congressional candidate Cait Conley told CNN's "State of the Union" that she would not campaign alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani or Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., but did not directly answer whether Democrats should reject the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

The group's influence in New York has become an issue in her bid to unseat Republican Rep. Mike Lawler. Anchor Dana Bash asked Conley whether she would campaign alongside Mamdani or Ocasio-Cortez after noting Lawler has sought to link his opponent to the Democratic Party's socialist wing.

"No, Dana, I‘m good up here making the case to the voters in the New York 17th Congressional District," Conley said.

'DAMNING SILENCE': SWING-SEAT DEMOCRAT STAYS QUIET AFTER AOC VOICES SUPPORT

Lawler's campaign manager, Ciro Riccardi, told Fox News Digital on Sunday that Conley's appearance demonstrated why the campaign has criticized her over debates and accused her of failing to distance herself from the DSA.

"Now everyone is seeing why Cait Conley has ducked and dodged debate challenges with Congressman Lawler. She’s incapable of answering direct questions without showing her true colors," he said. "Cait Conley’s refusal to disavow Zohran Mamdani and the DSA is disqualifying. She is just as extreme as the rest and that was exposed today for all to see, including embracing impeachment."

Lawler previously told Fox News Digital that he challenged Conley to six debates after her Democratic primary victory, while Conley's campaign said she agreed to two debates hosted by local networks.

Bash separately pointed to Rep. Tom Suozzi’s, D-N.Y., calls for his party to confront the DSA and asked Conley whether she agreed. Conley did not directly state whether she believed Democrats should reject the organization, instead discussing political division within both parties.

DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’

"I look at what we’re trying to do, which is unite this country where we have seen partisanship to include partisanship within our own party — absolutely divide people to render government dysfunctional," Conley said. "What we have to focus on is how do we bring people together, and right now, what I see coming out of Washington is corruption on both sides, extremism on both sides that is fueling hate, fueling dysfunction."

Suozzi has taken a more explicit position toward the socialist organization, telling Fox News Digital in August that Democrats would have to address the DSA's influence and reject its policy positions.

"I don't ascribe to any of those ideas at all, and I think that there's very little support for those ideas," Suozzi said.

SOCIALISM VS CAPITALISM: HOUSE DEMS CLASH OVER WHAT NY ELECTION RESULTS MEAN FOR PARTY

The DSA's national program calls for abolishing ICE and ending detention and deportations. It also advocates redirecting police funding as steps toward "fully abolishing the police and prison system," universal rent control, publicly owned social housing and universal government-funded healthcare.

Lawler’s campaign has previously pressed Conley over her relationship with the Democratic Party’s progressive wing after Ocasio-Cortez congratulated Conley on winning the Democratic primary in June. Riccardi at the time challenged Conley to state whether she rejected Ocasio-Cortez and other candidates associated with the party’s left flank.

"Which is it, Cait: do you reject AOC and the candidates who want to abolish ICE, defund the police, and tear down our borders, or do you embrace them?" Riccardi said.

Conley, a 16-year Army veteran who served on former President Joe Biden's National Security Council, won a crowded Democratic primary in June and is challenging two-term incumbent Lawler in a closely watched Hudson Valley contest that could determine control of the House.

Fox News Digital reached out to Conley for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Autonomous excavators are digging with empty cabs
item.description: Bedrock Robotics says its autonomous excavators are doing paid earthwork on active job sites in Texas and Nevada with no operator in the cab.
item.content:encoded:
If you have ever driven past a construction site and watched an excavator moving huge piles of dirt, you probably figured there was an experienced operator sitting in the cab. On some job sites in Texas and Nevada, there is nobody in that seat.

San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics has autonomous excavators doing real commercial earthwork with no operator onboard. The company says the deployments follow a year of testing on active job sites with human supervision.

Seeing AI take over software tasks is one thing. Watching it control a massive excavator on a live construction site feels very different. Bedrock says this could help contractors deal with worker shortages and keep projects moving more efficiently. Here's how the technology works and what could come next.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS

Bedrock says its operator-free excavators are now active on major infrastructure projects. One machine is working on a Nevada water treatment facility with Sundt Construction. In Texas, Bedrock is working with Champion Site Prep on a multimillion-cubic-yard earthwork project.

The company also has a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation. The current work centers on rough early earthmoving and foundation prep.

The company is concentrating on clearing earth, cut-and-fill operations and rough cuts before moving into more detailed work. That makes sense because earthwork comes early in a project. If crews fall behind there, everything that follows can feel the delay.

Bedrock measures excavator productivity by the cubic yards of earth moved during a shift, a company spokesperson tells CyberGuy.

How much earth a machine should move depends on the project, soil conditions and the rest of the equipment involved. Still, the spokesperson says, "As of our deployments in August 2026, two years after the company was founded, we are already near human-level productivity."

Bedrock calls its system the Bedrock Operator. The company designed it as a retrofit for existing heavy equipment. Bedrock says crews can install its sensor and computing package in a day without permanent changes to the machine. Once a site manager sets the initial plan, the software takes over the digging work. Bedrock says its machine-learning system can understand the surrounding area and plan movement. It can then carry out complex tasks.

The company says it trained the system on tens of thousands of hours of field work. However, there is an important detail about the current rollout. Bedrock is deploying new excavators that it outfitted and tested at its own facilities. When we asked when the system would begin operating on contractors' existing equipment, a Bedrock spokesperson said the company has no update to share yet but hopes to have more soon. So the retrofit model remains central to Bedrock's plan. The live operator-free deployments are still in an earlier phase.

Seeing a huge excavator move with nobody inside will probably make some people nervous. Bedrock knows safety will help determine how far this technology goes and says it comes first as the company expands deployment. The machines monitor their own progress while they work. If a machine gets stuck or cannot continue, the system can call for help.

When we asked how often a person needs to step in, a Bedrock spokesperson told CyberGuy, "It's relatively rare." If a machine encounters something unusual or gets stuck, someone monitoring the fleet can briefly intervene until the autonomous system is ready to take back over.

Bedrock also keeps a person in the loop. That gives the system a path to human support without requiring someone to sit in the cab all day. On active sites, that becomes especially important. People walk through work zones. Water trucks and other heavy equipment move nearby.

Bedrock says the safety response happens automatically. "If a person or unauthorized object gets too close to a Bedrock-equipped machine, the machine will automatically stop," the spokesperson said. The excavator stays stopped until the person or object has moved to a safe distance, with no manual intervention required.

HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN

Bedrock picked excavators for a reason. The company says excavators can account for about 25% of a contractor's fleet. They also take years to master.

Bedrock estimates that an operator may need five years or more to fully develop the skill. That creates a difficult staffing problem. Contractors need experienced people, yet many projects involve long stretches of repetitive earthmoving.

Bedrock wants autonomous equipment to handle more of that repeatable production work. Skilled operators could then focus on detailed jobs or supervise a larger operation.

We have seen autonomous excavators before. CyberGuy previously covered HEAP, a 12-ton robotic excavator that built a massive stone wall on its own.

What makes Bedrock different is where the technology is headed now. These excavators are doing commercial work on active job sites as part of real infrastructure projects.

The timing helps explain why investors are pouring money into this technology. Bedrock has raised more than $350 million. Its founding team includes former Waymo engineers who spent years working on autonomous vehicles.

Meanwhile, construction companies are struggling to find enough skilled workers. Bedrock cites industry estimates showing that roughly one in five construction workers is over age 55. Another estimate says more than 40% of the construction workforce could retire within the next five years.

The company also points to research showing that 92% of firms with open craft positions have difficulty filling at least some of those jobs. Those departures could hit contractors while demand remains high across many types of building projects.

Costs add another pressure point. Bedrock cites a McKinsey analysis that found large construction projects typically took 20% longer than scheduled and ran up to 80% over budget.

Then there is safety. Construction accounts for a disproportionate share of workplace deaths compared with its share of the overall workforce. Automation could help reduce exposure to dangerous tasks. However, companies will still need to prove that autonomous machines can work safely around people over long periods.

Bedrock also takes a firm position on what this technology means for equipment operators. "We do not expect operators to be replaced at all," a Bedrock spokesperson tells CyberGuy. In the near term, the company sees Bedrock-equipped machines working alongside existing crews because contractors do not have enough skilled operators to tackle every project. Longer term, Bedrock expects some experienced operators to move into supervisory positions overseeing autonomous equipment. The company compares that future role to becoming a "foreman for machines." At the same time, Bedrock says people who want to continue operating equipment themselves should still have a place in construction for years to come.

The long-term idea goes far beyond one excavator digging by itself. Bedrock wants multiple machines to coordinate across a job site. Bedrock co-founder Kevin Peterson described a future where an excavator could work alongside a bulldozer, truck and grader.

Instead of each machine operating as a separate tool, software could help coordinate the larger job. That could change project scheduling in a big way. A site manager might eventually assign the goal while a connected fleet determines how to move the work forward.

Bedrock says this coordinated model remains on its roadmap. For now, the company is scaling excavator deployments and expanding the types of tasks its system can perform.

Here's why this could affect you. Construction delays can hold up new housing, road projects and water infrastructure. If autonomous equipment can keep earthwork moving when contractors cannot find enough experienced operators, some projects could move faster and stay closer to schedule.

Bedrock says it sees autonomous machines working alongside people rather than eliminating operator jobs. In the near term, that could give existing crews more help with repetitive earthwork. Over time, some experienced operators could end up supervising groups of autonomous machines while others continue working directly in the cab.

Permits and material shortages can still slow a project down. Skilled workers also remain essential for planning, detailed work and handling situations the technology cannot manage on its own.

I'll be watching whether that near-human productivity holds up as these machines move onto more job sites. Bedrock says human intervention is relatively rare today, but I also want to see how that changes when one person is monitoring a larger fleet.

Safety will be the other big test. I want to see what happens when something unexpected enters the work zone. The more autonomous equipment we put around people, the more important that real-world track record becomes.

What catches my attention here is that Bedrock has moved beyond showing what an autonomous excavator might be able to do someday. These machines are already doing paid work on active construction sites with nobody sitting in the cab. Bedrock now tells us the machines are nearing human-level productivity and that human intervention is "relatively rare." Those are encouraging signs, but I want to see how those claims hold up across more projects and over longer periods. I also like hearing Bedrock say directly that it does not expect operators to disappear. If autonomy helps contractors handle more work while experienced people take on tougher jobs or supervise the machines, there could be a real upside for both crews and the projects they build. The real test will come as Bedrock puts more of these machines to work. If they stay safe and productive around real crews, those empty cabs may become a much more familiar sight.

If autonomous machines could help finish construction projects faster, would you be comfortable seeing them on job sites, or would you worry about what they could mean for workers? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Sanders pushes 'death penalty' for crucial US industry that could give advantage to foreign adversaries
item.description: Progressives on Capitol Hill are pushing a proposal to ban artificial superintelligence, but critics warn the move could hand global tech dominance over to China and Russia.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, introduced legislation Thursday seeking to hit American artificial intelligence developers with a "corporate death penalty" and up to 20 years in prison— a move critics warn will hand a crucial edge in the global AI arms race to Beijing and Moscow.

The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would temporarily halt advanced AI development and establish a Cabinet-level federal agency authorized to oversee the physical destruction of non-compliant tech systems, likening advanced AI creation to the unlawful development of nuclear weapons. The measure explicitly targets systems capable of matching or exceeding human cognitive performance—specifically outlawing any AI model that exhibits the capacity to subvert shutdown commands, execute unauthorized cyberattacks, or undermine the U.S. government.

But while progressives frame the measure as an urgent check on "AI oligarchs," experts are warning that imposing sweeping criminal penalties on U.S. firms will severely handicap domestic innovation, while foreign adversaries will be able to continue expanding their capabilities unchecked.

FETTERMAN ALIGNS WITH TRUMP ON AI PUSH, WARNS CHINA BENEFITS FROM US 'OVERREACTION'

"If the United States stops developing advanced AI, China is unlikely to follow. Surrendering the lead in a potentially transformative technology would carry serious economic and national security costs," Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), a leading nonpartisan tech-innovation policy think tank, said in response to Sanders' proposal.

"A permanent, unilateral ban on all research into superhuman AI is too broad," added Gary Marcus, an AI expert who has testified on the matter before the U.S. Senate. He added that the proposed law was "a guarantee" the U.S. would be left behind when it comes to artificial intelligence advancements, describing it as "not the right approach," even though he said there were some aspects of the proposed bill that were "defensible."

REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES

Under the provisions of the legislation, the proposed criminal and corporate penalties are modeled directly after existing federal statutes governing the unlawful development of nuclear weapons.

Tech companies found attempting to circumvent the federal prohibition would face a "corporate death penalty"—an unprecedented enforcement mechanism that strips a firm's legal authority to conduct business in the United States. Individual software engineers, researchers or executives found in violation could face up to 20 years in federal prison.

DEM SENATOR PRESSES OPENAI, ANTHROPIC FOR ANSWERS IN AI HACKING PROBE

To enforce the ban, the legislation creates a new Cabinet-level federal AI agency tasked with monitoring frontier systems. The agency would be granted sweeping authority to intervene in tech operations, including physically supervising the removal of dangerous code and overseeing the physical destruction of non-compliant superintelligent hardware and infrastructure.

The bill also establishes criteria for what constitutes a banned system, specifically outlawing any AI model capable of planning or executing the "disempowerment of humanity." That includes software that exhibits the capacity to overthrow the U.S. government, carry out unauthorized cyberattacks or ignore human shutdown commands.

CRACKDOWN ON CRITICAL TECH COULD OPEN AMERICANS TO A NEW NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

Industry advocates, however, argue that resorting to extreme criminal sanctions ignores the practical realities of tech infrastructure and risk management.

"Knee-jerk policymaking is never a good thing, and I think that’s exactly what this proposal boils down to," said Aden Hizkias, associate policy director at Chamber of Progress, a tech industry coalition. "AI is an incredible tool that can improve millions of lives, but as AI skepticism grows, it’s on companies to earn trust and prove they are good neighbors. That means transparent construction agreements, bringing their own power generation, and making sure they're meeting environmental standards."

Fox News Digital reached out to Sanders' office for comment regarding concerns that the legislation would hand an AI edge to foreign adversaries like China and Russia, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

item.title: Missouri foster mom accused of trading teen for monkey avoids prison
item.description: Brenda Deutsch received a suspended sentence after allegedly trading a foster teen for a monkey, as the judge called her actions reprehensible.
item.content:encoded:
A Missouri foster mother accused of trading a teenage girl for a monkey avoided prison time, even as a judge condemned her as reprehensible and apologized to her alleged victims for a foster care system he said had failed them.

Brenda Deutsch, 70, was sentenced to seven years in prison for child endangerment, but a Lincoln County judge suspended execution of the sentence and placed her on three years of probation, allowing her to remain free if she complies with its terms, FOX2 St. Louis reported.

Judge Thomas Frawley also revoked Deutsch’s foster care license from the bench and criticized the state of Missouri for allowing her to keep it.

FLORIDA COUPLE ALLEGEDLY HELD FOUR CHILDREN IN TRACTOR-TRAILER CAB FOR NEARLY SIX YEARS

Frawley then apologized to the victims in the courtroom, telling them he was sorry the system had failed them.

Deutsch’s biological daughter, Brina Johnson, who testified about alleged abuse, said the outcome was not what she had hoped for.

"I’m kinda lost for words because this is not the end we wished for," Johnson told FOX2.

Johnson said a teenager present in the courtroom was the foster child at the center of allegations that Deutsch traded her for a monkey.

"I have the whole conversation on my phone, which I turned over to the detectives," Johnson said.

"That’s what she did; she had at least seven monkeys," Johnson said. "That’s just her thing. But she wasn’t any nicer to those monkeys than she was to a child."

Deutsch was arrested in April after authorities investigated allegations that she sent the foster child, who is now 17, to Texas to stay in a home Deutsch admitted in court she knew nothing about.

Court documents previously obtained by Fox News Digital said the investigation began after Deutsch sought permission to take the girl to visit a friend in Texas. Five days later, an anonymous caller alerted the Missouri Department of Social Services Children’s Division that Deutsch was allegedly physically and mentally abusing the child.

Investigators later learned of an allegation that the girl had been traded for an exotic animal and was living in Texas.

69 LIVE ANIMALS FOUND STUFFED IN PILLOWCASES IN HIDDEN CAR COMPARTMENT AFTER BORDER ARREST: FEDS

The teenager told investigators Deutsch informed her Texas friend that the friend could keep the child, but Deutsch "will be keeping the check," according to court documents.

A witness told police the girl had been left in an unsanitary Texas home filled with exotic animals. She was eventually taken into the custody of child protective services in Texas.

The teenager also described alleged abuse by Deutsch, telling investigators she was struck with objects including a paddle and shoes. During one alleged beating, she said she lay on the floor and tried to "soften the strikes to her body," according to court documents.

Deutsch also allegedly took away the girl’s clothes and once threatened to kill her "if she did not shut up," the documents said.

Deutsch declined to comment outside the courthouse, shielding her face with a piece of paper as she walked to her vehicle and drove away.

Deutsch has reportedly fostered more than 200 children over the years.

Johnson said the judge’s acknowledgment of the system’s failures offered some validation despite her disappointment with the outcome.

"It was good to know somebody knows from the other side of the street, that this shouldn’t have happened," Johnson said. "None of it should. And the system did fail us, failed them all."

Fox News Digital's Julia Bonavita contributed to this report.

item.title: West Virginia angler lands 72.75-pound blue catfish to set new state record on the Ohio River
item.description: Tyler Harmon's casual Ohio River outing with his dad and 4-year-old son turned into a 72.75-pound blue catfish that set a new West Virginia state record.
item.content:encoded:
Tyler Harmon wasn't exactly chasing history when he loaded up the boat for a casual evening of fishing with his dad and 4-year-old son.

In fact, his expectations were considerably smaller.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

The Ravenswood, W.Va., angler had gotten the urge to hit the Ohio River late in the day, so he brought his son, Walker, and his father, Rodney, along.

The mission was to find something small enough for Walker to catch himself.

"We were just kind of out there hoping to catch a small catfish for my boy to reel in," Harmon told Jackson County, West Virginia’s 13 News.

Instead, they ended up with a 72.75-pound monster.

The Harmons set up in a familiar stretch of the Ohio River near Ravenswood, with four catfish rods spread behind their 18-foot aluminum boat. Tyler had previously found submerged trees and brush in the area, and the water was roughly 25 to 30 feet deep.

GEAR UP FOR FALL WITH LABOR DAY DEALS ON HUNTING, FISHING AND CAMPING ESSENTIALS

They hadn't been fishing long when things got interesting.

A barge rolled through, its wake pulling the boat's anchor loose and sending the Harmons drifting. Around that time, one of the rods doubled over.

At first, Rodney thought they were snagged. Then, the line started moving upriver.

"It just started stripping drag," Tyler said. "I was like, ‘We’re not stuck on anything. That’s a fish.’"

And not a small one.

Tyler spent roughly 20 minutes battling the blue catfish, trying to keep his 40-pound test line away from submerged brush and the boat's anchor line as the fish repeatedly worked around the front of the boat.

"Whenever it surfaced the first time, my boy saw it and started flipping out thinking it was a shark," Harmon said.

Close enough.

CHARTER CAPTAIN JONATHAN MOSS EXPLAINS HOW TO GET KIDS HOOKED ON FISHING FROM AN EARLY AGE

Rodney grabbed the landing net, but the catfish was so heavy it bent the aluminum handle. They eventually managed to hoist the fish into the boat together.

Once it hit the deck, Tyler realized this might be more than just the biggest fish of his life.

"I was like, ‘We gotta get this thing weighed,’" he said.

The problem, though, was that it was late on a Friday night.

Tyler began calling around trying to reach the state fisheries personnel needed to certify a record, but nobody was available. So the Harmons shifted into fish-preservation mode.

On the run back to the ramp, they repeatedly dumped buckets of river water over the catfish to keep it alive. Rodney then raced home for a livestock tank, which they filled with river water and equipped with an aerator.

Eventually, Tyler contacted a friend who owns D&D Bait Shop nearby, where the fish could spend the night in a larger tank with a better aeration system.

The next morning, a West Virginia fisheries official arrived with a certified scale.

The numbers were ridiculous: 72.75 pounds, 48.15 inches long and 33.5 inches around.

That was enough to establish a new West Virginia state weight record for blue catfish, surpassing the 71-pound fish Michael Ramey caught from the same Ohio River area in May.

And to make things even sweeter, the catch could also be worth $20,000.

Harmon was using a Hellcat rod made by Catch The Fever, which runs a promotion offering cash awards to anglers who catch qualifying state-record fish with its equipment. The company said it was still reviewing the paperwork and requirements as of Sept. 1, but the fish appeared to qualify for the full payout.

Tyler admitted that's actually one of the reasons he bought the rod in the first place.

"I was like, ‘Hey, I’m gonna go buy one of these just in case,’" he said, "because you never know."

If the payout becomes official, Harmon said he plans to use the money toward a down payment on a new house.

The record fish, meanwhile, didn't end up on anyone's dinner table or wall. After officials finished weighing and measuring it, Harmon returned the giant blue catfish alive to the Ohio River near where it was caught.

He said he may eventually have a replica mount made.

Tyler is already thinking about that next one, too. His new goal is West Virginia's flathead catfish record — a mark that has stood for roughly 70 years.

Why not, right?

item.title: Mamdani under fire after symbolic 9/11 pen goes to former al Qaeda defense lawyer
item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces backlash for handing a 9/11 ceremonial pen to aide Ramzi Kassem, who represented a convicted al Qaeda member.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing backlash after giving a ceremonial pen from a 9/11 remembrance ceremony to a top aide who once represented a convicted al Qaeda member whose brother-in-law hijacked the plane that struck the Pentagon.

Mamdani signed executive orders Friday ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, designating the date a citywide day of remembrance and service and strengthening efforts to prevent future terrorist threats.

After signing the final order, Mamdani handed the pen to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and asked her to pass it to chief counsel Ramzi Kassem. Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, who pleaded guilty to war-crime charges tied to al Qaeda plots against commercial ships and was the brother-in-law of Khalid al-Mihdhar, one of the hijackers aboard American Airlines Flight 77, which crashed into the Pentagon, killing 184.

MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?'

The handoff drew criticism on social media, with users arguing on X that Kassem’s role in the ceremony distracted from an event meant to honor those killed in the attacks and the first responders who died trying to save them.

"This is a slap in the face to victims ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11," wrote podcaster Benny Johnson on X.

FLASHBACK: MAMDANI TORCHED FOR RECYCLING 9/11 TRIBUTES AFTER YEARS OF NEAR-IDENTICAL POSTS

"I sincerely hope the rest of the country understands just how hard it is to be in New York City with this mayor, and especially as we’re approaching this most serious and solemn day for NYC: 9/11," wrote former New York state Senate candidate Maria Danzilo.

Another user on X called it a "deliberate gesture by Mamdani that undermines 9 / 11 yet again with impunity."

ACCUSED 9/11 MASTERMIND KHALID SHEIKH MOHAMMED, 3 CO-DEFENDANTS SET FOR 2028 TRIAL

City Hall told the New York Post that Kassem attended the ceremony because he and his team drafted both executive orders as part of his duties as chief counsel.

That role has drawn scrutiny because Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, a Guantánamo Bay detainee who pleaded guilty to war-crime charges tied to al Qaeda plots against commercial ships, including the 2002 bombing of a French oil tanker off Yemen’s coast. Al-Darbi’s sister was married to Khalid al-Mihdhar, one of the hijackers aboard the plane that crashed into the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001.

Kassem also founded a CUNY legal clinic that provides free representation to Muslims and represented Mahmoud Khalil, a leader of the pro-Palestinian encampment at Columbia University who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: LSU fans boo Jayden Daniels during jumbotron tribute after NIL cease-and-desist dispute
item.description: Jayden Daniels was booed during an NFLSU video at Tiger Stadium after reportedly sending LSU a cease-and-desist letter over his name and likeness.
item.content:encoded:
Jayden Daniels was phenomenal during his two seasons under center for the LSU Tigers and took home every award imaginable, including the Heisman Trophy, during his final campaign in Death Valley in 2023. He should be an LSU legend for life.

The keyword in the previous sentence is "should," and many Tigers fans let their opinion about the former signal caller be known during their team's 51-10 beatdown of Clemson on Saturday night.

During a break in the action at Tiger Stadium, an "NFLSU" video began playing on the jumbotron, highlighting the former LSU players currently playing in the NFL. Every player, except for one, got at least a slight pop from the fans when their names appeared on the video board.

LSU HAD A REVIVAL, CLEMSON WAS AT A FUNERAL: LANE KIFFIN’S DEBUT SENDS A LOUD MESSAGE TO COLLEGE FOOTBALL

When Daniels' name appeared alongside former LSU linebacker K'Lavon Chaisson, a teammate of Daniels with the Washington Commanders, the cheers quickly turned into booing.

The harsh reaction by some LSU fans towards Daniels comes after he and his attorney, Adam Kenner, reportedly sent a cease-and-desist letter to the university in August, arguing that the Tigers couldn't continue using his name, image, and likeness.

"Accordingly, LSU must immediately cease and desist from any further issue, use, display, publication, distribution, promotion, commercialization, or other exploitation of Mr. Daniels' NIL in any manner or medium," Kenner wrote in a letter to LSU athletic director Verge Ausberry. "Any use of Mr. Daniels' NIL occurring after LSU's receipt of this notice will be deemed knowing and willful and will be pursued vigorously through all available legal and equitable remedies, without further notice."

JAYDEN DANIELS WANTED ‘RESPECT’ FROM LSU. INSTEAD, HE STARTED AN UGLY FIGHT THAT WILL TARNISH HIS REPUTATION

Daniels wore No. 5 during his time in Baton Rouge, and sophomore cornerback DJ Pickett is wearing the same digit this season for the Tigers. Pickett has claimed that he has worn the No. 5 jersey throughout his career and that it was also promised to him when he signed with the Bayou Bengals.

Brian Kelly, who was fired as the head coach at LSU, coached Daniels during his time at LSU and was also a primary recruiter of Pickett.

Lane Kiffin has taken over the program as the head coach in 2026 and has no ties to Daniels during his time in Baton Rouge, as Kiffin was the head coach at Ole Miss at the time.

After Daniels won the Heisman Trophy in 2023, it became incredibly likely his No. 5 jersey would be retired by the Tigers, but LSU has a five-year waiting period before discussions of retiring numbers can take place.

Daniels appears to have been under the impression that LSU should have asked him beforehand whether he was okay with another player wearing No. 5 for the first time since he left Baton Rouge for the NFL.

Joe Burrow, who won the 2019 Heisman Trophy and led LSU to a national title, has not had his No. 9 worn by another player in Baton Rouge since being drafted first-overall by the Cincinnati Bengals in 2020.

item.title: William Fichtner has ‘never’ regretted turning down roles and refuses to cross ‘certain lines’ in Hollywood
item.description: William Fichtner told Fox News Digital that he's never regretted turning down a role if it crosses his boundaries, even if they end up being successful.
item.content:encoded:
"Lucky" star William Fichtner has no problem turning down a role if it crosses his boundaries.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 69-year-old actor shared that he has "never" regretted saying no to a project, even if it turned out to be a big success.

"I've been a bit pickier and choosier at moments in my life where I probably didn't have a right to be," he said. "But if I didn't believe it, if I didn't think that I could do something with it, and there are certain lines that I just don't cross. But, if I don't have a belief in it, then I have a little bit of a fear that I don't want to be bad, and I just won't take the journey."

He explained that he doesn't "hold it as a badge of honor," that he has said no to a few "jobs that were really good money," and described knowing immediately that "this isn't happening" when reading something he doesn't like.

NICOLAS CAGE TURNED DOWN PARTS IN TWO BIG FRANCHISE MOVIES FOR ROLES HE THOUGHT WERE BETTER

"Then my wife looks at me and goes, 'You like it, right?' And I'm like, 'Actually, it's in the garbage, honey. Sorry. Are we going to the store now? We've got to go to Costco, right?'" he said.

Fichtner plays Wayne Whittaker in the Apple TV miniseries "Lucky,' which aired its series finale, titled "All Good Things," on Wednesday, Aug. 19.

The show stars Anya Taylor-Joy as Luciana "Lucky" Armstrong, a reformed criminal who is forced to engage in unlawful activities one last time, in order to secure her freedom and permanently leave behind her former life of crime.

She's going to throw some things at me and there's a curveball in there that is like, OK, all right, I gotta give this woman her due. This is really good."

When it came time to filming the chaotic scene, Fichtner joked that when he arrived on set and saw "this very beautiful, petite woman standing there with these incredible eyes that look right through you," he thought, "We're in the middle of all of this like havoc and this did that," referring to Taylor-Joy.

Fichtner started his acting career in the 1990s, going on to become one of the most recognizable supporting actors of the 2000s. His most recognizable role is FBI Special Agent Alexander Mahone in "Prison Break," which he starred in from 2006 to 2009.

Having worked on both a miniseries and a series with multi-season arcs, he was able to compare how he prepared for each.

"Working on 'Prison Break.' You could be finishing up season two, episode 10. Your last shooting day is on a Wednesday and Wednesday afternoon you get episode 11 and you start tomorrow," he said. item.title: Michigan fans called out on social media for rushing field after Wolverines steal win over Western Michigan
item.description: Michigan fans stormed the field after Bryce Underwood's Hail Mary saved a 13-12 win over Western Michigan, sparking college football debate.
item.content:encoded:
Emotions are what make college football great, but there is a fine line between showing raw emotions and letting emotions get the best of you. The latter happened in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on Saturday night.

The Michigan Wolverines were beaten – and some would say literally – by Western Michigan on Saturday before one of the more unbelievable scenes in the sport's history unfolded.

After Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood sailed his Hail Mary attempt out of the back of the endzone and the clock hit triple zeros, the officials reviewed the play and elected to put one second back on the clock. The video review seen on the NBC broadcast left no doubt that time had expired on the clocks available to the network, but a second was added, and the rest is history.

CLOCK CONTROVERSY ALLOWS MICHIGAN WOLVERINES TO AVOID MASSIVE UPSET AGAINST WESTERN MICHIGAN

Underwood's second Hail Mary attempt was perfect as he lobbed a pass to the goal line for 6-foot-4 receiver JJ Buchanan to go up and get it, and get it he did.

With Michigan stealing a 13-12 win over the Broncos in dramatic fashion, the fans who stuck around in The Big House stormed the field to celebrate. While the Wolverines have gone through a significant amount of change in leadership and coaching in recent months, it's still the same Michigan that is just three years removed from winning a national title, and its fans rushing the field after beating a MAC team was quite the scene.

The Wolverines were four-touchdown favorites heading into Saturday's contest against the Broncos.

College football fans were quick to call out the celebrations that broke out on the field in Ann Arbor.

While the last-second drama added some much-needed fuel to a relatively lackluster Week 1 of college football, the addition of time back on the clock, coupled with a fanbase of a blue-blood program storming the field after scoring 13 points against a MAC, turned into the headline as opposed to the final play itself.

Michigan welcomes Oklahoma to town in Week 2. It goes without saying that the Wolverines will need to improve in a hurry if they want to compete against the Top 10 Sooners.

item.title: Texas deputy screams and runs after 'dead' deer springs to feet in viral encounter

item.content:encoded:
An East Texas sheriff’s deputy got the scare of his life when a deer he thought was dead suddenly sprang to its feet, sending the startled lawman screaming back toward his cruiser in a moment caught on camera that quickly went viral online.

The wild encounter was captured on the deputy’s dashcam and shared on Facebook by Trinity County Sheriff Woody Wallace, who joked that sometimes things can "scare the heck out of a person."

Wallace had some fun with the incident, encouraging social media users to "[w]atch when he encounters what he thinks is a dead deer until it comes back to life!"

The video opens with the deputy approaching what appears to be a motionless doe lying along the side of the road.

BIG SKY, MONTANA WILDLIFE ENCOUNTER CAUGHT ON VIDEO AS MOOSE CHARGES TOWARD WOMAN AND HER DOGS

As the deputy gets closer to examine the animal, the deer suddenly springs to life.

The startled deputy lets out a scream and races back toward his patrol vehicle.

"OK, we’re good," the deputy says with a laugh after recovering from the surprise.

The deer is last seen sitting up on the side of the road before the video ends.

LATE-NIGHT BULL RUN ENDS WITH A LITTLE COWBOY KNOW-HOW ON BUSY CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY

"Instead of a citation, the ‘suspect’ made a four-legged getaway and vanished into the East Texas woods," Wallace wrote on Facebook.

Wallace later assured viewers that the doe was unharmed and "made a full recovery."

item.title: Bessent predicts oil prices could drop as low as $40 after Iran conflict ends and supply floods market
item.description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted oil prices could drop to between $40 and $50 after the Iran conflict ends, citing massive supply ready to hit the market.
item.content:encoded:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted oil prices could fall to between $40 and $50 per barrel once the Iran conflict ends, arguing that abundant supply is poised to hit the market after constraints ease.

Bessent asserted that the American economy is "very strong" and even accelerating, saying that the country is experiencing a "productivity burst" during an interview on "My View with Lara Trump."

"On the other side of this, we actually could see oil prices $40 or $50 because there's so much supply coming on. It's just constricted right now," he told Fox News host Lara Trump.

IRAN WARNS SHIPS OF 'FORCEFUL RESPONSE' AS US-BACKED HORMUZ ROUTE CHALLENGES TEHRAN'S GRIP

"So my message is: Underlying economy is very strong. Job growth is strong. Wage growth is strong."

The "energy supply shock" is only temporary, Bessent said, calling the United States an "energy superpower" and a leader in artificial intelligence and global computing power.

BESSENT CREDITS TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICIES WITH HELPING RETURN JOBS TO AMERICANS AS WAGE GAINS RESUME

"Americans, on average, are breaking even. Working-class Americans at the bottom of the wage spectrum are doing a little better than inflation, but we don't believe that that is acceptable," the Treasury chief said.

"But what is the good news is that these wage increases are going to keep going. We've got a manufacturing renaissance, a construction renaissance. So the wages will keep going, this war will end, and those will turn into real wage gains."

LIZ PEEK: THE TRUMP ECONOMY IS DOING BETTER THAN THE MEDIA WANT TO ADMIT

Bessent's comments come as tension between Washington, D.C., and Tehran show no sign of cooling following Saturday’s U.S. strikes on Iranian tankers.

He predicted that the Strait of Hormuz would soon become less crucial to global oil trade as Gulf nations work to construct alternative pipeline routes that will allow them to circumnavigate the tumultuous waters, diminishing Iran's ability to threaten oil flows.

"This is the greatest economic isolation operation in the history of the world. We are going to asphyxiate this regime," Bessent said, adding that the combination of the blockade and sanctions is "one of the most powerful one-two punches in the history of economic isolation."

"I think we are going to get to the other side of this Iran conflict with a safer world, with an Iran that cannot have a nuclear weapon, and that we are in the lift-off phase."

item.title: Terry Bradshaw opens up about mortality after beating cancer twice: 'Am I going to heaven?'
item.description: Terry Bradshaw reveals how two cancer diagnoses reshaped his Christian faith and marriage in a raw podcast interview ahead of his new memoir release.
item.content:encoded:
Pro Football Hall of Famer and longtime "FOX NFL Sunday" co-host Terry Bradshaw opened up Wednesday on William Shatner and Melanie Shatner Gretsch's "No Time But Now" podcast about confronting his mortality after battling two forms of cancer, explaining how the health scares deepened his Christian faith and changed the way he approaches his marriage, family and remaining years ahead of the release of his new memoir.

"My thoughts were about dying. Am I going to heaven? Am I a good enough man? Have I been a good enough Christian? Have I been kind to people? Am I going to heaven?" Bradshaw said.

Bradshaw's reflections followed two cancer diagnoses that he previously disclosed publicly in 2022. Fox News Digital reported at the time that Bradshaw was diagnosed with bladder cancer in November 2021 and underwent surgery and treatment at Yale University Medical Center. Months later, an MRI prompted by neck pain revealed a Merkel cell tumor, a rare form of skin cancer, in his neck.

DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES

Bradshaw recounted on the podcast that he initially kept his first diagnosis private and focused on whether doctors believed it could be treated rather than dwelling on the possibility of dying.

"I didn't feel panic. I didn't think death. I'm pretty sure I said, ‘Well, curable.’ Yeah. The doctor thinks in six weeks," Bradshaw said. "And so I never once went, ‘Oh, I got to get my house in order. I got to do this.’ I just said, ‘OK, curable.’ That's what I needed to hear."

The second diagnosis came shortly after Bradshaw completed treatment for bladder cancer. He said doctors found Merkel cell cancer in his parotid gland area, leading to surgery that removed 27 lymph nodes followed by six weeks of radiation treatments.

WILLIAM SHATNER AND DAUGHTER MELANIE REVEAL THEY BATTLED STAGE 4 CANCER AT THE SAME TIME

The National Cancer Institute describes Merkel cell carcinoma as a "very rare" skin cancer that tends to grow quickly and can spread at an early stage, frequently beginning on sun-exposed areas, including the head and neck.

Bradshaw told Shatner that although he understands cancer could return, his faith helped shape how he views death.

"No, death did not frighten me. It did not in any way frighten me. Now, that's easy to say because I haven't been told, 'You're dying. Well, you're going to die,'" Bradshaw said.

"I know I'm going to die. And when that time comes, how will I handle that with grace and strength and an understanding that God loves me? I'm going to go to heaven. I'm going to see my family again with it. Yes, that's going to be my, that's going to be my strength," he continued.

JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS

The former Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback said surviving cancer also changed how he approaches life with his wife, Tammy, including a desire to travel more and spend their time together differently.

"I want her to have more happiness than she ever thought possible. To me, that just makes, that fills my spirit. That fills me with joy," Bradshaw said.

"To know that, you know, that I'm a good husband now. I'm a good husband now. And I've got a great wife and I want her to know what it's like to really feel loved."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Bradshaw's comments came ahead of the Oct. 13 release of "Looking for Terry: A Memoir," his first memoir in more than two decades. Publisher Harper Select said the book will examine Bradshaw's battle with cancer, depression, faith and the public persona he developed during more than five decades in football and television.

Bradshaw was the No. 1 overall pick in the 1970 NFL Draft and led Pittsburgh to four Super Bowl championships, winning Super Bowl MVP twice before his 1989 induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He remains a co-host of "FOX NFL Sunday," with FOX Sports confirming Bradshaw's return for the 2026 NFL season.

item.title: 8 everyday things that would quit working without data centers
item.description: Data centers power everything from streaming and gaming to AI chatbots and fraud detection. Here's how they quietly run the apps you use daily.
item.content:encoded:
Data centers are the largely unseen infrastructure behind modern life, powering everything from the apps on your phone and shows you stream to online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence.

Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Most Americans may never see one, but they rely on them constantly, often without realizing it.

"Data centers have been around for as long as technology has been around," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you’re touching technology and using everything from social media to your email, all of that information, all of the data is being processed in a data center."

As more of the economy moves online, data centers have become far more than a niche piece of the tech industry. They are increasingly essential infrastructure for everyday American life. The U.S. is home to roughly 4,000 operational facilities, with thousands more planned or under construction as demand for cloud computing and AI accelerates.

Here are eight ways data centers quietly power the services Americans rely on every day.

From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind the services people use every day. When you open an app, upload a photo, refresh your feed or send a message, your phone is connected to servers that retrieve and deliver that information in seconds.

The apps may live on a screen in your hand, but much of the work happens far away inside a physical facility filled with computers running continuously.

Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and other streaming platforms rely on massive computing infrastructure to deliver movies, videos and music to millions of users at once. Data centers help store enormous libraries of content and move it quickly enough to prevent the pauses and buffering that frustrate viewers.

ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM

Online games also rely on data centers to connect players, synchronize what is happening in a match and reduce the lag that can make a game unplayable. The more people stream, game and use data-heavy services, the more computing power those platforms need behind the scenes.

Your iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups do not just float around in cyberspace. They are stored on physical servers inside data centers, often with copies kept in multiple locations to help prevent data loss.

That means a lost phone or broken laptop does not necessarily mean lost memories or work file — but it also means the cloud depends on vast amounts of real-world hardware.

Search engines rely on data centers to sort through enormous amounts of information and return results in fractions of a second. Every query triggers systems that locate relevant webpages, images, maps, videos and other information before sending the results back to your device.

What feels like a simple Google search is actually a complex exchange between your device and powerful servers processing requests at an enormous scale.

When you order something online, data centers help manage inventory, process payments, make product recommendations and track packages to your door. They also allow retailers to update product availability and pricing quickly as demand changes.

ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI

During major shopping events such as Black Friday, those systems have to handle a surge of shoppers and transactions without crashing.

Google Maps, Waze and other navigation services depend on computing infrastructure to process traffic patterns, routes and location data in real time. They combine information from roads, users, businesses and mapping systems to estimate travel times and suggest alternate routes.

Without the data centers behind them, navigation apps would not be able to react as quickly to accidents, congestion or changing road conditions.

Video calls, cloud-based software, shared documents and workplace messaging all rely heavily on data-center infrastructure. Every Zoom meeting, Slack message and live edit to a shared file depends on servers that keep information synced between people working from different locations.

THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS

For many companies, data centers have become as essential to day-to-day operations as office space, phones and electricity.

Every time someone asks an AI chatbot a question, generates an image or uses an AI-powered search feature, data centers provide the computing power working behind the screen. Those requests require far more processing than a basic web search because the systems must analyze information and generate a response in real time.

That is a major reason the technology industry is racing to build bigger and more powerful data centers, often equipped with specialized chips designed for AI workloads.

In addition, autonomous vehicles, advanced robotics, scientific research and other emerging technologies require increasingly powerful computing infrastructure. Data centers help train the AI systems behind those tools, process huge volumes of data and support the software that allows them to improve over time.

item.title: Angry locals block famous beach as mass tourism protests escalate at vacation hot spot
item.description: Around 100 residents occupied Cala Saladeta beach in Ibiza to protest tourist overcrowding, demanding that locals reclaim the island's public spaces from visitors.
item.content:encoded:
Some 100 residents staged an occupation of a beach in Ibiza recently to protest overtourism amid growing frustration over mass tourism in Spain — and more action is apparently planned. 

The group gathered at Cala Saladeta, a popular tourist beach, last week, according to Balearic public broadcaster IB3.

The protest was organized by the Ibiza Youth Association, a local youth group.

INFLUENCERS REACHING PEAK BACKLASH AFTER SUMMER OF RUINED DESTINATIONS AND EXPERIENCES FOR AMERICANS 

Ibiza is one of Spain's Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean Sea.

The island is visited by many tourists, with its population swelling during the summer months.

Known to locals as Eivissa, Ibiza received nearly 1.2 million tourists in the second quarter of 2025, according to data from the Balearic Islands Statistics Institute.

Organizers rallied "against tourist overcrowding," IB3 reported, and activists handed out watermelon as part of a demand "that residents be able to enjoy the island's public spaces."

CRUISE SHIP CRACKDOWN HITS TOURIST HOT SPOT AS CITY FAST-TRACKS NEW VISITOR TAX

The group said in its manifesto that "our land and our culture are being directly pushed out of public spaces, and increasingly out of private spaces, as well, displayed solely as tourist attractions," according to local outlet CadeNA SER.

The manifesto also decried a tourism model catering to "wealthy foreigners and famous partygoers," while arguing that housing, food and other living costs have become unaffordable for residents.

"[Young people are] fed up with not being able to enjoy [the island] as tourists do, because we believe we can no longer continue giving up spaces to the visitors brought by this extractive tourism model, which makes our lives in Ibiza more precarious," the manifesto added, per Cadena SER.

The island's coves, which attract tourists during the busy summer season, were also a focus of the group's manifesto.

"We have decided that we want to reclaim places of tranquility, including during the summer," the statement added.
